Introduction Pleural infection is a bacterial infection of the pleural space that most often develops as a complication of pneumonia, although non-pneumonic and healthcare-associated sources also occur. It represents a clinical continuum extending from complicated parapneumonic effusion, in which infected or highly inflammatory fluid requires drainage, to frank empyema, defined by macroscopically purulent pleural fluid. Because cultures are frequently negative, diagnosis cannot rely on microbiology alone and is supported by pleural-fluid acidity or hypoglycaemia, loculation or septation, and compatible clinical and radiological findings [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]. Progressive inflammation promotes fibrin deposition, compartmentalisation, and, in advanced disease, pleural organization that can restrict lung expansion.

Pleural infection remains an important cause of hospital admission, prolonged treatment, and death. Population-based studies have reported increasing incidence over recent decades, particularly among older men; in Finland, the overall incidence was 23.4 episodes per 100,000 person-years and rose during the study period [ 4 ]. Across published adult cohorts, approximately three-quarters of patients have at least one comorbidity, the median hospital stay is about 19 days, and reported mortality varies substantially according to population, case definition, and follow-up [ 5 ]. Large tertiary-care cohorts and prospective studies further show that adverse outcomes are concentrated among older patients and those with greater comorbidity, renal dysfunction, hypoalbuminaemia, or high Renal, Age, Purulence, Infection source, Dietary factors (RAPID) scores [ 6 , 7 ].

The clinical course is heterogeneous. Some patients improve with antibiotics and drainage, whereas others require repeated procedures, intrapleural therapy, intensive care, or thoracic surgery. Current management is based on prompt antimicrobial therapy and adequate source control, with image-guided chest-tube drainage for established complicated effusion or empyema [ 1 , 2 ]. In selected patients with poorly draining loculated infection, combined intrapleural tissue plasminogen activator and deoxyribonuclease improves radiographic clearance and can reduce surgical referral and length of stay [ 8 ]. Surgery remains necessary when medical source control fails or when advanced pleural organization prevents lung re-expansion. The relative use and timing of these strategies vary between centers, reflecting differences in case mix, expertise, and access to thoracic surgery [ 1 , 2 ].

Microbiological diagnosis is clinically important because pathogen identification may permit targeted antimicrobial therapy, yet conventional pleural-fluid culture has limited sensitivity. Previous antibiotic exposure, specimen handling, culture technique, anaerobic recovery, and the use of blood-culture bottles or molecular methods can materially influence diagnostic yield [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ]. The causative spectrum also varies by geography and acquisition setting. Community-acquired disease is commonly associated with streptococci, oral anaerobes, and polymicrobial infection, whereas healthcare-associated or nosocomial disease more often includes Staphylococcus aureus , Enterobacterales, non-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli, and antimicrobial-resistant organisms [ 9 , 10 , 11 ]. Recent cohorts from North Africa and Southeast Asia have confirmed substantial regional differences in culture positivity, pathogen distribution, and resistance patterns, reinforcing the need for locally derived microbiological data [ 12 , 13 ]. A negative pleural culture therefore does not exclude pleural infection and may identify a clinically distinct, rather than simply less severe, subgroup.

Despite expanding evidence, several uncertainties remain. Studies comparing microbiologically positive and negative pleural infection have produced inconsistent findings. A recent bicentric cohort reported higher mortality among patients with pleural-fluid microbiological positivity [ 14 ], whereas another phenotyping study found important clinical differences but no independent association between culture positivity and mortality after adjustment [ 15 ]. A Danish multicenter cohort likewise observed similar short-term mortality in patients with known and microbiologically negative etiology [ 16 ], while a large surgical cohort found longer intensive-care and postoperative stays in culture-positive disease but similar short- and long-term survival [ 17 ]. These differences may reflect variation in referral pathways, sampling practices, acquisition setting, pathogen prevalence, treatment, and outcome definitions. Moreover, systematic reviews show that much of the available evidence comes from selected geographic regions and that microbiology is strongly context-dependent [ 5 , 9 ]. Contemporary, clinically integrated data from Romania and Eastern Europe remain limited, and international initiatives continue to identify regional variation in etiology, management, and outcomes as a major knowledge gap [ 18 ]. A well-characterized real-world cohort from this region can therefore provide information that is not readily transferable from other healthcare systems.

The primary objective was to compare the clinical, pleural-fluid, radiological, treatment, and in-hospital outcome profiles of adults with a positive versus negative aerobic culture from the first clinically relevant pleural specimen. Secondary objectives were to describe pathogen and resistance distributions by acquisition setting, quantify the timing and overlap of composite-outcome components, and estimate the adjusted association between PF-positive status and a major adverse in-hospital outcome.

2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Study Design and Setting This was a single-center, retrospective observational cohort study with consecutive inclusion, conducted at the “Victor Babes” Infectious Diseases and Pneumoftiziology Hospital, a tertiary referral hospital that covers the population of four counties in western Romania. All adult admissions between 1 January 2017 and 31 December 2025 were screened. The unit of analysis was the index hospitalization for pleural infection; repeat admissions for the same episode were not counted separately. Follow-up extended from admission until discharge, transfer, or in-hospital death. The study was designed and reported in accordance with the STROBE statement and the RECORD extension for studies using routinely collected health data.

Candidate records were identified through a multisource search of discharge-diagnosis labels (empyema, pyothorax, pleural infection, complicated parapneumonic effusion, and parapneumonic effusion), pleural-fluid laboratory accessions, thoracentesis and chest-drain registers, ward admission/discharge lists, and thoracic-surgery transfer documentation. Candidates were linked by hospital identifier and admission dates and manually validated. The historical screening log retained the combined search concepts but not the exact diagnosis-code list, SQL syntax, or finer exclusion categories. Consequently, the cohort is described as case-ascertained rather than independently verifiable consecutive inclusion. Of 368 candidates, 51 were excluded under the single archived reason ‘source record unavailable or insufficient to verify eligibility or outcome’.

2.2. Study Population Eligible patients were aged 18 years or older, had imaging-confirmed pleural effusion, and had a documented lower respiratory or pleural infectious syndrome treated with antibacterial therapy. For adjudication, a compatible syndrome required clinician-documented infection plus systemic inflammatory evidence (fever/hypothermia, leukocyte abnormality, elevated inflammatory markers, or sepsis) and respiratory/pleuritic symptoms or compatible pulmonary imaging. At least one pleural-infection criterion was also required: frank pus; positive pleural Gram stain or culture; pleural-fluid pH ≤ 7.20; pleural-fluid glucose ≤ 40 mg/dL (≤2.2 mmol/L); loculation/septation; pleural contrast enhancement, split-pleura sign, or intrapleural air in the appropriate clinical setting; or an explicit diagnosis of empyema/complicated parapneumonic effusion confirmed by clinical adjudication.

Exclusions were uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion, isolated tuberculous pleuritis without bacterial superinfection, non-infected malignant or other non-infectious effusion, isolated post-pneumonectomy empyema, repeat admission for a continuous unresolved episode, and insufficient information. A new episode required documented clinical/radiological resolution followed by a new infection; otherwise, only the first hospitalization was retained. Primary parapneumonic infection accompanied pneumonia and lacked a preceding pleural/thoracic procedure; postprocedural infection followed direct pleural instrumentation or thoracic surgery. Community-acquired infection had an event date no later than hospital day 2 without qualifying recent healthcare exposure. Healthcare-associated infection had community-onset timing plus at least one of: acute-care hospitalization for ≥2 days in the preceding 90 days; long-term-care residence; or intravenous therapy, chemotherapy, wound care, or hemodialysis in the preceding 30 days. Nosocomial infection had an event date on or after hospital day 3, with admission as day 1.

2.3. Data Sources and Collection A standardized data dictionary was used to abstract electronic and paper records. Baseline clinical and serum laboratory values were the first available within 24 h of admission; pleural variables came from the first clinically relevant pleural sampling episode; treatments and outcomes covered the index hospitalization. A primary abstractor entered the data. Thirty-seven of 317 records (11.7%) underwent source-record re-verification during routine quality control; this check was not blinded, the selection mechanism was not retained in the audit log, and paired reviewer-level fields were unavailable, so inter-rater agreement could not be calculated. Thirty-three records flagged as requiring clinical adjudication were reviewed using the prespecified criteria; unresolved disagreements between two clinicians were referred to a third investigator. Range, date-order, logical-consistency, and cross-field concordance checks were applied before analysis.

2.3.1. Clinical, Laboratory, and Imaging Variables Collected variables included demographics, residence and institutionalization, comorbidities, Charlson Comorbidity Index, admission physiology, oxygen support, altered mental status, sepsis/septic shock, RAPID score, and routine serum measurements. Imaging was abstracted from the first relevant radiology report, with source-image review when needed. General findings included effusion size and laterality, loculation/septation, intrapleural air, consolidation, cavitation, malignancy suspicion, and fistula. Pleural effusion size was classified according to the original radiology report. On chest radiography, effusions explicitly described as large or massive were assigned to the corresponding category; no fixed quantitative threshold based on hemithorax occupation was applied. Size classification from other imaging modalities was likewise based on the corresponding radiology report. CT-specific findings were analyzed only when CT was recorded as the primary imaging modality; non-CT-primary records were treated as not evaluable rather than negative for pleural enhancement, split-pleura sign, and necrosis/abscess.

2.3.2. Pleural-Fluid and Microbiological Assessment Pleural specimens were obtained during routine care and submitted in a sterile container, inoculated into blood-culture bottles, or both (108, 75, and 93 patients, respectively, in the primary cohort). The recorded sampling-to-laboratory interval was available for 146/276 patients and was generally under 2 h. Gram stain and aerobic and anaerobic cultures were performed as ordered under the laboratory standard operating procedures in force at the time. Species identification and antimicrobial susceptibility results were abstracted from final validated reports. Susceptibility interpretation used the EUCAST clinical breakpoint table valid on the test date: versions 7.1 (2017), 8.0/8.1 (2018), 9.0 (2019), 10.0 (2020), 11.0 (2021), 12.0 (2022), 13.1 (2023), 14.0 (2024), and 15.0 (2025). Specific culture media, incubation durations, bottle brands, and identification/AST instrument models were not consistently recoverable across the nine-year period and were not inferred. For an exploratory comparison of aerobic culture positivity by specimen collection method, patients were grouped according to whether blood-culture bottles were used (alone or in combination with sterile-container submission) or specimens were submitted exclusively in sterile containers.

The qualifying specimen was the earliest pleural-fluid specimen during the index hospitalization with an interpretable aerobic culture. PF-positive status required a positive aerobic pleural culture, and PF-negative status required a negative result; an unperformed test was never coded as negative. Gram stain, anaerobic culture, blood/sputum/bronchoalveolar-lavage cultures, and operative specimens were descriptive and did not determine the primary exposure. Urinary antigen testing was not systematically captured in the study database and was therefore not included in the microbiological analyses. Seven operative specimens were positive, but all seven patients were already PF-positive from an earlier aerobic pleural culture; operative-only positivity was therefore zero. Polymicrobial infection required at least two organisms from the qualifying episode. MDR, XDR, and PDR followed the ECDC/CDC expert definitions: non-susceptibility to at least one agent in at least three categories; non-susceptibility in all but two or fewer categories; and non-susceptibility to all agents in all categories, respectively. ESBL and carbapenemase phenotypes were accepted only when explicitly reported after contemporaneous EUCAST-compliant testing; mechanisms were not inferred from susceptibility patterns. Common skin flora were considered pathogens only with a compatible sterile-site syndrome and concordant Gram stain, repeat isolation, or clinician adjudication; otherwise, they were excluded as probable contaminants. No PF-positive record was flagged as a probable contaminant. Pleural-fluid pH was abstracted from the final laboratory record. Syringe type, analyser model, documentation of air/local-anesthetic contamination checks, and the pH-specific processing interval were not retained consistently; no values were imputed, and this pre-analytic uncertainty was considered in interpretation.

2.3.3. Treatment, Source Control, and Outcomes Antimicrobial variables included the initial regimen, anaerobic and MRSA coverage, changes after microbiological results, concordance with the antibiogram, and intravenous/total treatment duration. Antibiotic exposure before pleural sampling was defined by documented pre-admission treatment or an in-hospital antibiotic start date earlier than the culture date; same-day order was not inferred. Source-control variables included thoracentesis, drain placement, type, caliber and guidance, repeat procedures, intrapleural therapy, VATS, thoracotomy, decortication, and transfer for thoracic surgery. Surgical transfer meant transfer to a thoracic-surgery service or hospital specifically for operative pleural source control. Operative procedure type after transfer was abstracted from available transfer/return documentation, but surgery dates were not retained.

The primary clinical outcome was a major adverse in-hospital composite comprising at least one of in-hospital death, ICU admission/transfer, or thoracic surgery/surgical transfer. ICU present on the admission date counted ( n = 10). All events recorded during the index hospitalization counted in the principal association analysis; therefore, that analysis is phenotypic rather than strictly prognostic. Dates of the qualifying culture, ICU admission, surgical transfer, and death were compared at the patient level. Same-calendar-day sequence was classified as indeterminate. A strict-temporality sensitivity cohort excluded any patient whose qualifying sample was collected on or after a recorded component. A second sensitivity outcome counted only components occurring strictly after the sample. For transferred patients, follow-up for nonfatal events ended at transfer; post-transfer surgery type was captured when documented, whereas post-transfer ICU events and death were not systematically available. Component-specific results and overlap were prespecified as prominent secondary analyses.

2.4. Ethical Considerations The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The protocol was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee of the “Victor Babes” Hospital of Infectious Diseases and Pneumophysiology, Timisoara, Romania (approval no. 7595, 29 July 2026). Data were pseudonymized before analysis, the re-identification key was stored separately, and access was restricted to authorized investigators.

2.5. Statistical Analysis No a priori sample-size calculation was performed because all verified eligible episodes were included. The 317-patient cohort was used for flow and case-definition summaries. The primary comparison was restricted to the 276 patients with an interpretable first aerobic pleural culture: 127 PF-positive and 149 PF-negative. Species and resistance analyses were restricted to PF-positive episodes with test-specific denominators. As an exploratory assessment of sample-size sensitivity, we estimated the minimum absolute difference in composite-event proportions detectable with 80% power using the fixed PF-positive and PF-negative group sizes, a two-sided significance level of 0.05, and the observed PF-negative event rate as the reference probability. This calculation used a normal approximation for two independent proportions without continuity correction and was not intended to assess power for the adjusted model.

Categorical variables are reported as n/N (%) and continuous variables as mean (standard deviation) or median [interquartile range]. Age, temperature, and systolic blood pressure were compared using Welch’s t test; other continuous variables used the Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical comparisons used Pearson’s chi-square or Fisher’s exact test when expected counts were sparse. Multicategory pathogen comparisons used the Fisher–Freeman–Halton test with Monte Carlo estimation (1,000,000 replicates; fixed seed 20260720). Unadjusted odds ratios (ORs) and 95% Wald confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for clinically relevant binary comparisons.

The prespecified maximum-likelihood logistic model included age (per 10 years), sex, Charlson Comorbidity Index, healthcare-associated/nosocomial versus community acquisition, urea (per 10 mg/dL), albumin (per 0.5 g/dL decrease), C-reactive protein (per 50 mg/L), loculation/septation, purulent fluid, and PF-positive status. Covariates were entered simultaneously without automated selection. All 276 patients had complete model data; no imputation was used. Model convergence, separation, and functional form of continuous terms were assessed. Collinearity among model predictors was further evaluated using variance inflation factors (VIFs) calculated from the predictor matrix. Particular attention was given to healthcare-associated/nosocomial acquisition and serum albumin, with VIF values greater than 5 considered indicative of potentially problematic collinearity.

Sensitivity analyses restricted the PF-negative group to episodes without extrapleural microbiological evidence, restricted the cohort to primary parapneumonic infection, added admission year, required the qualifying sample to precede every recorded composite component, redefined the outcome to include only strictly post-sampling components, and expanded sampling eligibility to any interpretable aerobic or anaerobic pleural culture. The post-sampling and expanded-culture analyses were added in response to review and are exploratory. Component-specific and acquisition/phenotype analyses were unadjusted.

Missingness and evaluable denominators were reported for each variable. No outcome was imputed. All tests were two-sided, and p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant; secondary and sensitivity analyses were exploratory and no multiplicity correction was applied. Analyses were performed using SPSS version 26 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA).

3. Results 3.1. Cohort Assembly and Baseline Characteristics Of 368 potentially eligible records, 51 were excluded because the source record was unavailable or insufficient to verify eligibility or outcome. The descriptive cohort comprised 317 patients. Forty-one had no interpretable aerobic pleural culture and were excluded from the primary comparison. The primary analytic cohort therefore included 276 patients: 127 (46.0%) PF-positive and 149 (54.0%) PF-negative. Among the 149 PF-negative patients, 19 had microbiological evidence from extrapleural specimens, whereas 130 had no recorded microbiological identification from the evaluated specimens. Extrapleural results did not alter the primary pleural-culture classification.

The cohort was predominantly male, with substantial comorbidity. Most infections were community-acquired, and loculation or septation was common. CT was the primary imaging modality in 139/276 (50.4%) patients. Detailed baseline characteristics are presented in Table 1 , and data availability is summarized in Supplementary Table S1 .

PF-positive patients were more frequently institutionalized (28/127 [22.0%] vs. 9/149 [6.0%]; p < 0.001), had higher Charlson scores (3 [2–5] vs. 2 [1–3]; p < 0.001), and more often had chronic kidney disease (38/127 [29.9%] vs. 20/149 [13.4%]; p < 0.001). Acquisition distribution differed ( p = 0.008), principally because nosocomial infection occurred in 29/127 (22.8%) PF-positive versus 14/149 (9.4%) PF-negative patients. Frank empyema was also more frequent (75/127 [59.1%] vs. 62/149 [41.6%]; p = 0.004).

Among 215 patients with pleural biochemistry, PF-positive cases had lower pH (6.94 [6.78–7.11] vs. 7.20 [6.98–7.33]; p < 0.001) and glucose (23.5 [15.2–32.0] vs. 40.0 [28.0–51.0] mg/dL; p < 0.001). Consolidation was less frequent in PF-positive patients (81/127 [63.8%] vs. 115/149 [77.2%]; p = 0.014). CT-specific denominators did not show group differences in pleural enhancement, split-pleura sign, or necrosis/abscess ( Table 1 ).

3.2. Microbiological Findings Aerobic pleural culture was positive in 54/98 (55.1%) healthcare-associated/nosocomial and 73/178 (41.0%) community-acquired episodes (OR 1.77, 95% CI 1.08–2.89; p = 0.025). Within the primary cohort, Gram stain was positive in 120/230 (52.2%) tests performed and anaerobic culture in 38/213 (17.8%). Aerobic pleural-culture positivity was observed in 80/168 (47.6%) patients whose specimens were inoculated into blood-culture bottles, either alone or together with sterile-container submission, compared with 47/108 (43.5%) patients whose specimens were submitted exclusively in sterile containers (OR 1.18, 95% CI 0.73–1.92; p = 0.505). The difference was not statistically significant. This exploratory comparison should be interpreted cautiously because collection methods were determined by routine clinical practice rather than a standardized paired protocol ( Table 2 ).

Antibiotic exposure before pleural sampling was present in 202/276 (73.2%) patients and did not differ by PF status or acquisition group. Blood-culture bottles were used for 168/276 (60.9%) pleural samples. Positive blood and sputum/bronchoalveolar-lavage cultures were documented in 70/276 (25.4%) and 53/276 (19.2%) patients, respectively.

Among 127 PF-positive episodes, 58 (45.7%) were Gram-positive, 54 (42.5%) were Gram-negative, and 15 (11.8%) were mixed. Streptococci accounted for 31 (24.4%), Enterobacterales for 30 (23.6%), other Gram-negative organisms for 19 (15.0%), Staphylococcus aureus for 18 (14.2%), mixed pathogens for 15 (11.8%), other organisms for 9 (7.1%), and anaerobes for 5 (3.9%). Enterobacterales or other Gram-negative organisms were recorded in 30/54 (55.6%) healthcare-associated/nosocomial versus 19/73 (26.0%) community-acquired PF-positive episodes.

Fifteen PF-positive episodes (11.8%) were polymicrobial and 107/127 (84.3%) had a full antibiogram. An MDR phenotype was recorded in 26/127 (20.5%), including 16/54 (29.6%) healthcare-associated/nosocomial and 10/73 (13.7%) community-acquired episodes ( p = 0.028). MRSA occurred in 3/18 S. aureus episodes. Among 37 episodes with explicit marker results, ESBL and carbapenemase phenotypes were recorded in 10 (27.0%) and 7 (18.9%), respectively ( Supplementary Table S2 ). Operational definitions used throughout the revised analyses—including cohort eligibility, PF classification, acquisition setting, microbiological and resistance phenotypes, surgical transfer, and timing-sensitive outcomes—are summarized in Supplementary Table S3 .

3.3. Antimicrobial Treatment and Pleural Source Control Grouped initial antimicrobial regimens did not differ significantly by PF status ( p = 0.064). The most frequent individual regimens were ceftriaxone plus metronidazole (52/276 [18.8%]), piperacillin-tazobactam (51/276 [18.5%]), ampicillin-sulbactam (31/276 [11.2%]), and meropenem (31/276 [11.2%]). All patients received initial anaerobic coverage, and 59/276 (21.4%) received MRSA coverage. Regimens were changed in 76/127 (59.8%) PF-positive and 70/149 (47.0%) PF-negative patients ( p = 0.033). Among 107 PF-positive episodes with an evaluable antibiogram, 79 (73.8%) regimens were concordant.

Median intravenous antibiotic duration was 14 [8–18] days and was longer in PF-positive than PF-negative patients (16 [12–21] vs. 11 [7–16] days; p < 0.001). Total duration was 24 [19–32] days overall, 28 [21–33] days in PF-positive patients, and 22 [18–30] days in PF-negative patients ( p < 0.001). Thoracentesis was performed in all 276 patients, and a chest drain was inserted in 242 (87.7%), with no difference by PF status. Among drained patients, the median time from admission to drainage was 1 [0–3] day, 53/242 (21.9%) required repositioning, and 58/242 (24.0%) underwent repeated drainage.

Overall intrapleural treatment use was similar between groups, but the choice of agent differed: combined tPA–DNase was more frequently used in PF-positive patients, whereas tPA alone was more common in PF-negative patients ( Table 3 ). VATS was recorded in 13/276 (4.7%), thoracotomy in 11/276 (4.0%), and decortication in 15/276 (5.4%). VATS and thoracotomy were mutually exclusive, and their union exactly matched the 24 surgical transfers; every transferred patient had one recorded operative approach, and decortication was nested within these procedures. Transfer frequency did not differ by PF status (12/127 [9.4%] vs. 12/149 [8.1%]; p = 0.682).

3.4. Clinical Outcomes and Length of Stay The composite outcome occurred in 111/276 (40.2%) patients: 54 (19.6%) died in the hospital, 59 (21.4%) had ICU admission/transfer, and 24 (8.7%) underwent thoracic surgery/surgical transfer. Components overlapped; the first recorded component was ICU admission/transfer in 58 patients, surgical transfer in 19, and death in 34 ( Supplementary Table S4 ).

The composite occurred in 60/127 (47.2%) PF-positive and 51/149 (34.2%) PF-negative patients (OR 1.72, 95% CI 1.06–2.80; p = 0.028). PF-positive patients had higher in-hospital death (34/127 [26.8%] vs. 20/149 [13.4%]; OR 2.36, 95% CI 1.28–4.35; p = 0.005) and ICU admission/transfer (36/127 [28.3%] vs. 23/149 [15.4%]; OR 2.17, 95% CI 1.20–3.90; p = 0.009). Surgical transfer did not differ (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.52–2.75; p = 0.682).

The qualifying sample preceded ICU admission in 34/59 ICU events, occurred on the same day in 14, and followed ICU admission in 11; 10 ICU events were present on the admission date. The sample preceded surgical transfer in 23/24 events and occurred on the same day in one. It preceded death in 53/54 events and occurred on the same day in one. The strictly post-sampling composite occurred in 95/276 (34.4%) patients, including 54/127 (42.5%) PF-positive and 41/149 (27.5%) PF-negative patients ( p = 0.009).

Median length of stay was 17 [12–28] days overall and did not differ by PF status. Mechanical ventilation was recorded in 68/276 (24.6%; p = 0.060 by PF status) and vasopressor support in 71/276 (25.7%; p = 0.043). Thirty-day mortality remained an exploratory available-case outcome because status was missing for a substantial proportion ( Supplementary Table S1 ).

3.5. Factors Associated with the Major Adverse In-Hospital Outcome The principal model included 276 patients and 111 events ( Table 4 ; Figure 1 ). PF-positive status was associated with the composite before adjustment (OR 1.72, 95% CI 1.06–2.80; p = 0.028), while the adjusted estimate was 1.60 (95% CI 0.94–2.74; p = 0.084). The principal model describes associations across the index hospitalization and is phenotypic rather than strictly prognostic. Healthcare-associated/nosocomial acquisition was associated with the composite after adjustment (aOR 1.76, 95% CI 1.03–3.00; p = 0.038). The adjusted estimate per 0.5 g/dL albumin decrease was 1.21 (95% CI 0.99–1.49; p = 0.060). The overall likelihood-ratio test was p = 0.040. In an exploratory two-proportion sensitivity calculation, the available group sizes provided approximately 80% power to detect a 16.6-percentage-point difference in composite-event rates, compared with the observed difference of 13.0 percentage points. Collinearity diagnostics showed VIFs of 1.07 for healthcare-associated/nosocomial acquisition and 1.09 for serum albumin. The maximum VIF among all model predictors was 1.31, indicating no problematic multicollinearity.

PF-positive estimates remained directionally consistent after restriction to the strictly microbiology-negative reference (aOR 1.74, 95% CI 0.99–3.05), primary parapneumonic episodes (aOR 1.54, 95% CI 0.87–2.74), and adjustment for admission year (aOR 1.62, 95% CI 0.95–2.78). In the strict-temporality sensitivity analysis, which excluded patients whose qualifying pleural sample was collected on or after any recorded outcome component, 249 patients remained (84 events), yielding an aOR of 1.54 (95% CI 0.86–2.76; p = 0.145). When only strictly post-sampling components were counted, the exploratory aOR was 1.77 (95% CI 1.01–3.09; p = 0.045).

In secondary analyses, the composite occurred in 48/98 (49.0%) healthcare-associated/nosocomial and 63/178 (35.4%) community-acquired episodes (OR 1.75, 95% CI 1.06–2.89; p = 0.028), and in 50/137 (36.5%) frank empyema versus 61/139 (43.9%) non-purulent CPPE episodes (OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.45–1.19; p = 0.211). Within PF-positive episodes, the outcome did not differ materially between Gram-negative and Gram-positive infection or between polymicrobial and monomicrobial infection.

4. Discussion 4.1. Principal Findings and Clinical Interpretation In this nine-year retrospective cohort, aerobic pleural-culture positivity identified a clinically distinct subgroup characterized by greater comorbidity, more frequent nosocomial acquisition and frank empyema, and more pronounced pleural biochemical abnormalities. PF-positive patients experienced higher unadjusted rates of adverse in-hospital outcomes, although the adjusted association between culture positivity and the composite outcome remained uncertain. Healthcare-associated/nosocomial acquisition retained an adjusted association with the composite outcome. Culture positivity was also accompanied by more frequent antibiotic modification and longer treatment durations, without clear differences in pleural drainage or surgical transfer. Overall, these findings suggest that aerobic culture positivity reflects a combination of host vulnerability, acquisition setting, and disease phenotype rather than functioning as an isolated prognostic determinant [ 14 , 15 ].

The phenotype associated with PF positivity extended beyond the microbiological result itself. Its association with greater comorbidity, institutionalization, nosocomial acquisition, purulence, and more marked pleural acidosis could reflect a combination of host vulnerability, greater bacterial burden, more advanced pleural inflammation, differences in organism cultivability, and the timing of presentation and sampling. Our data cannot distinguish between these mechanisms. In unadjusted analyses, the composite outcome occurred in 47.2% of PF-positive and 34.2% of PF-negative patients; in-hospital mortality was approximately twice as frequent in the PF-positive group, and intensive-care admission and vasopressor use were also more common. Nevertheless, the adjusted association with the composite outcome was smaller and statistically imprecise (aOR 1.60, 95% CI 0.94–2.74). Its direction was retained when the reference group was restricted to strictly microbiology-negative episodes (aOR 1.74, 95% CI 0.99–3.05) and when the analysis was restricted to patients whose qualifying culture preceded every recorded outcome component (aOR 1.54, 95% CI 0.86–2.76). In the exploratory analysis that counted only components occurring strictly after pleural sampling, the estimate was somewhat larger (aOR 1.77, 95% CI 1.01–3.09). These estimates should be interpreted in the context of their different temporal eligibility criteria and outcome definitions. The principal model included all 276 patients and 111 composite events recorded during the index hospitalization, including events that preceded or coincided with pleural sampling. Specifically, ICU admission preceded sampling in 11 patients and occurred on the same calendar day in 14, for whom the within-day sequence remained indeterminate. The strict-temporality sensitivity analysis restricted the cohort to 249 patients whose qualifying sample preceded every recorded outcome component (84 events), whereas the post-sampling analysis retained all 276 patients but counted only outcome components occurring strictly after sampling (95 events). These differences in patient eligibility and event counts may explain variations in the adjusted estimates and their precision. Accordingly, the modest differences between models should not be interpreted as evidence of a definitive change in the underlying association between PF-positive status and adverse outcomes.

This pattern lies between the findings of previous cohorts. Wong et al. similarly found that microbiologically positive patients had greater comorbidity and institutional residence but reported an independent association with mortality and substantially higher three-month mortality [ 14 ]. By contrast, Chan et al. observed higher unadjusted mortality among culture-positive empyema cases, but culture positivity was not independently associated with mortality after adjustment [ 15 ]. Meyer et al. found no material differences in mortality, intensive-care admission, surgery, or treatment duration between patients with microbiology-negative infection and those with a known bacterial etiology, although their definition of known etiology was broader than direct pleural-fluid positivity [ 16 ]. In a highly selected surgical population, Cheng et al. reported longer postoperative hospitalization, intensive-care stay, and ventilation among culture-positive patients, but no difference in 30-day mortality or two-year survival [ 17 ]. Differences in case selection, microbiological definitions, temporal ordering, outcome periods, and adjustment strategies limit direct comparison. Overall, the available evidence indicates that PF positivity defines a clinically meaningful risk phenotype but does not yet establish it as a sufficiently robust standalone prognostic determinant [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ].

4.2. PF-Negative Pleural Infection and Diagnostiv Yield PF-negative infection accounted for 149/276 (54.0%) episodes in the primary analytic cohort. Of these, 130 were strictly microbiology-negative, and 19 had compatible microbiological evidence only from extrapleural specimens. In the overall cohort, 73.2% had received antibiotics before pleural sampling, and blood-culture bottles were used for 60.9% of pleural samples. Neither exposure differed materially by PF status. These observations should not be interpreted as evidence that antibiotic treatment or specimen-processing methods do not influence microbiological yield. Antibiotic exposure was observationally measured, and treatment intensity, duration, and exact sequencing relative to same-day sampling could not be fully reconstructed; moreover, blood-culture bottles were used according to routine practice rather than in a protocolized paired comparison of the same specimen. In a prospective paired study, Menzies et al. showed that adding blood-culture bottle inoculation to standard pleural-fluid culture increased pathogen identification from 37.7% to 58.5% [ 19 ]. A recent population-based cohort also demonstrated an inverse association between the duration of previous antibiotic therapy and culture positivity, suggesting that the extent of exposure may be more informative than a binary exposure measure [ 20 ].

Molecular methods further demonstrate that conventional culture-negative disease often remains microbiologically identifiable. In 90 culture-negative specimens, 16S rRNA PCR detected a plausible pathogen in 31%, particularly fastidious and anaerobic organisms, and most causative positive results directly influenced management [ 21 ]. In a prospective study of clinically confirmed pleural infection, targeted metagenomic sequencing was positive in 70% of patients, compared with 35% for conventional culture, and identified additional species and polymicrobial anaerobic infections [ 22 ]. Similarly, the TORPIDS analysis found polymicrobial bacterial profiles in most sequenced pleural infections, considerably expanding the organism spectrum detected by culture [ 23 ]. PF-negative disease should therefore not be equated with microbiological sterility or necessarily with less advanced infection. It probably comprises a mixture of lower-burden disease, antibiotic-suppressed infection, fastidious or anaerobic infection, and episodes in which the available methods failed to identify the causative organism. The 19 episodes with extrapleural evidence also show why direct pleural-culture status and broader etiological identification should remain analytically distinct [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ].

4.3. Microbial Ecology and Antimicrobial Resistance The microbiological profile differed substantially by acquisition setting. Streptococci were the most frequent individual pathogen group, whereas Enterobacterales and other Gram-negative organisms were more common in healthcare-associated/nosocomial infections (55.6% vs. 26.0% of PF-positive episodes), alongside a higher prevalence of multidrug-resistant phenotypes (29.6% vs. 13.7%). These findings are consistent with previous studies demonstrating geographical and acquisition-related variation in pleural infection microbiology [ 9 , 10 , 12 , 13 ]. Conventional cultures probably underestimate anaerobic and polymicrobial infection, as demonstrated by molecular studies [ 11 , 23 , 24 , 25 ]. Importantly, the recorded ESBL and carbapenemase proportions refer only to the 37 episodes with explicit marker results and cannot be generalized to the entire cohort. These observations support acquisition-specific empirical antimicrobial therapy informed by local resistance patterns.

4.4. Antimicrobial Treatment and Source Control Initial antimicrobial treatment was predominantly broad-spectrum and did not differ significantly between PF-positive and PF-negative patients, consistent with treatment being selected before pleural microbiological results became available. All patients received anaerobic coverage, while approximately one-fifth received empirical anti-MRSA therapy. By contrast, subsequent antibiotic modification was more frequent in PF-positive episodes, and treatment was concordant with the available antibiogram in 73.8% of evaluable cases. Microbiological identification therefore had a measurable influence on antimicrobial management, although maintaining broader coverage may have remained appropriate when polymicrobial infection, incompletely detected anaerobes, or concurrent extrapleural infection was suspected. Median intravenous and total treatment durations were 14 and 24 days, respectively, with PF-positive patients receiving longer courses than PF-negative patients. This difference probably reflects greater purulence, documented microbiology, comorbidity, or perceived disease severity rather than evidence that longer treatment is intrinsically more effective. In the SLIM trial, extending treatment from 14 to 21 to 28–42 days did not significantly reduce treatment failure among medically stabilized patients, while ODAPE suggested that two weeks of amoxicillin–clavulanate may be sufficient for carefully selected patients with stabilized community-acquired complicated parapneumonic effusion [ 26 , 27 ]. Both trials were small and enrolled selected populations, limiting their applicability to older, comorbid patients and those with nosocomial, resistant, or surgically managed infection.

Pleural drainage was performed in 87.7% of our cohort, generally within one day, and its use and timing were similar between microbiological groups. This supports source-control decisions based primarily on clinical, biochemical, and imaging evidence rather than culture status, as recommended by current guidance [ 1 , 2 ]. Available evidence also suggests broadly comparable outcomes with small-bore and large-bore drains, although dedicated randomized evidence remains limited [ 28 ]. Intrapleural treatment was administered to 46.7% of patients. Overall use was similar by PF status, although combined tPA-DNase was more frequent among treated PF-positive patients, and tPA alone was more frequent among treated PF-negative patients. MIST2 supports combined tPA-DNase, but not either agent alone [ 8 ]. Subsequent feasibility trials and meta-analyses have not yet established whether early intrapleural enzyme therapy or early VATS is generally superior: non-randomized studies suggest shorter hospitalization with VATS, but they are substantially affected by selection bias, while randomized studies have been too small for definitive efficacy comparisons [ 29 , 30 , 31 ]. Surgical transfer also did not differ by PF status. The exact equivalence between the 24 surgical transfers and the union of VATS and thoracotomy indicates complete overlap rather than separate additive events, with decortication nested within those procedures. Thus, treatment intensity in this cohort appears to have been driven mainly by the overall disease phenotype and response to initial drainage, whereas PF positivity had a clearer influence on antimicrobial modification and duration. Associations between individual interventions and outcomes cannot be interpreted causally because of confounding by indication.

4.5. Clinical Outcomes and Risk Stratification The clinical burden of pleural infection was substantial, with 40.2% of patients experiencing the composite outcome. PF-positive patients had higher unadjusted event rates, but the adjusted association remained imprecise, with a confidence interval including unity. Sensitivity analyses yielded directionally consistent estimates of varying precision. These findings do not establish equivalence between PF-positive and PF-negative disease and reinforce the need for larger studies with standardized sampling and outcome definitions [ 5 ].

Healthcare-associated or nosocomial acquisition was the only covariate with a conventionally significant adjusted association with the composite outcome (aOR 1.76, 95% CI 1.03–3.00). This variable may integrate resistant or difficult-to-treat pathogens, recent healthcare exposure, frailty, delayed recognition, and referral complexity. Lower serum albumin retained a directionally adverse estimate, with an aOR of 1.21 per 0.5 g/dL decrement, but the 95% confidence interval included unity. This direction is concordant with the RAPID model, in which albumin, age, renal function, infection source, and pleural-fluid purulence jointly stratify mortality risk [ 32 ]. RAPID was derived in MIST1 and initially validated in MIST2, while the prospective PILOT cohort reported three-month mortality of 2.3%, 9.2%, and 29.3% across low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups [ 7 , 32 ].

A subsequent Danish validation confirmed the gradient but reported corresponding risks of 2.4%, 17.0%, and 39.4%, illustrating that absolute risk varies between settings [ 33 ]. Albumin should therefore be regarded as an integrated marker of systemic inflammation, chronic illness, nutritional status, and physiological reserve, rather than as evidence that albumin replacement would alter outcome. Frank empyema was not associated with a higher composite-event rate in our secondary analysis, despite being more frequent among PF-positive patients. This is not necessarily paradoxical: purulence may prompt earlier recognition and drainage, and non-purulence, rather than purulence, contributes to the RAPID score [ 32 ].

Moreover, a multicenter CT cohort found no increase in 90-day mortality associated with loculation, whereas bronchopleural fistula carried a markedly less favorable prognosis [ 34 ]. Similarly, prospective PILOT analyses showed that sonographic septations influenced treatment decisions but were not independently related to mortality, surgery, or length of stay; pleural PAI-1, rather than septation itself, was associated with adverse outcomes [ 35 ]. Overall, host reserve, acquisition setting, and systemic illness may carry greater prognostic weight than purulence, loculation, or PF positivity considered in isolation. Neither albumin nor PF status should be used as a standalone decision rule, and the directionally consistent PF-positive estimates require evaluation in larger cohorts with standardized temporal assessment.

4.6. Clinical Implications Empirical antimicrobial treatment should reflect the acquisition setting and local resistance patterns. Streptococci and oral flora remain important in community-acquired infection, whereas Gram-negative and resistant organisms are more frequent in healthcare-associated/nosocomial disease. Anaerobic coverage remains appropriate because conventional culture incompletely identifies anaerobic and polymicrobial infections [ 1 , 2 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 23 , 24 , 25 ].

An interpretable pleural specimen should be obtained as early as clinically feasible, ideally before additional antibiotic exposure or escalation of care, and its timing relative to subsequent outcomes should be documented. PF positivity may identify patients with greater host vulnerability, more advanced pleural biochemical disturbance, and increased unadjusted risk, justifying close clinical surveillance and microbiology-guided treatment refinement. Conversely, PF-negative status should not be equated with the absence of bacterial infection or used to justify delayed drainage, inappropriately narrow empirical therapy, or less intensive monitoring.

Albumin may contribute to initial risk assessment when interpreted alongside age, renal function, acquisition source, physiology, and the broader clinical phenotype, but neither our model nor the RAPID literature supports using albumin as an isolated decision rule [ 7 , 32 , 33 ]. Finally, death, intensive-care admission, and surgery should be reported separately even when a composite is used, because surgery may represent definitive source control rather than clinical deterioration, and access to intensive care or thoracic services is system-dependent.

The principal strengths of this study include a nine-year cohort, classification based on the first interpretable aerobic pleural culture, explicit separation of direct pleural positivity from extrapleural microbiological evidence, and integration of clinical, biochemical, imaging, microbiological, therapeutic, timing, and outcome data. Test-specific and variable-specific denominators, explicit operational definitions, component-level outcome accounting, and sensitivity analyses addressing microbiological reference groups and specimen-to-outcome timing further strengthen interpretability. The study also provides uncommon contemporary data from Romania and Eastern Europe, where detailed pleural-infection cohorts remain limited. Its contribution is therefore not to define a universal treatment algorithm, but to provide local epidemiological and resistance data that may inform empirical prescribing, microbiological sampling pathways, organization of pleural source control, and the design of future outcome studies. The need for comparable regional data is recognized in systematic reviews, the ERS/ESTS statement, and the international INTERMITTENT initiative [ 2 , 9 , 18 ].

4.7. Limitations and Future Research Directions This study has limitations. Its retrospective, single-center design made case ascertainment and variable measurement dependent on existing clinical documentation. Exact diagnosis codes, query syntax, and granular reasons for the 51 exclusions were not preserved, so consecutive capture cannot be independently audited, and selection bias cannot be excluded. Generalizability to centers with different referral pathways, microbiological facilities, resistance patterns, or access to thoracic surgery is consequently limited. The primary analytic cohort also excluded 41 patients without an interpretable aerobic pleural culture. This restriction was necessary to define the exposure, but it creates a selected comparison population, and the findings should not be automatically extended to all patients with pleural infection.

Laboratory media, incubation duration, blood-culture-bottle brands, instrument platforms, and pH-specific pre-analytical procedures could not be reconstructed consistently across the nine-year period, although antimicrobial-susceptibility results were interpreted using the contemporaneous EUCAST standards applied by the hospital laboratory. Pre-sampling antibiotic exposure was common, blood-culture bottles were not used according to a uniform paired protocol, and anaerobic and molecular testing were incomplete. The PF-negative group is therefore etiologically heterogeneous, and misclassification resulting from antibiotic suppression, fastidious organisms, or limited diagnostic sensitivity may have attenuated between-group differences. CT-specific analyses used the conservative CT-primary denominator because the dataset did not identify every patient who underwent any CT.

The 37-record repeat check was not accompanied by a recoverable sampling scheme or reviewer-level agreement data, precluding a formal estimate of inter-rater reliability. Retrospective classification of community-acquired, healthcare-associated, and nosocomial episodes may also be imperfect despite the application of explicit operational criteria.

Clinical and laboratory practice, referral pathways, antimicrobial prescribing, use of tPA-DNase, and access to surgery or intensive care may have changed between 2017 and 2025. Adjustment for admission year did not materially alter the PF-positive estimate, but residual temporal confounding cannot be excluded. Treatment comparisons are particularly vulnerable to confounding by indication: patients receiving prolonged antibiotics, intrapleural therapy, or surgery are likely to differ systematically in disease severity, physiological reserve, microbiology, and response to initial drainage. The composite outcome also combines events with different clinical meanings. Death and intensive-care admission generally indicate adverse evolution, whereas surgery may represent both failure of initial medical treatment and successful definitive source control; intensive-care and surgical transfer are additionally influenced by eligibility, clinician judgment, bed availability, and local organization.

Although operative cultures did not create PF status and all seven operative-positive records were already positive on an earlier aerobic pleural culture, the principal exposure-outcome analysis was not fully prospective in temporal structure. Intensive-care admission preceded the qualifying sample in 11 patients, same-day sequence was indeterminate for some events, surgery dates were unavailable beyond transfer timing, and nonfatal follow-up ended at transfer. The post-sampling and strict-temporality analyses reduce particular sources of temporal ambiguity but use different event definitions or smaller effective samples and should be considered exploratory. Post-transfer intensive-care admission and death were not systematically captured. Thirty-day mortality was available only for a subset of patients, limiting the reliability of comparisons beyond hospitalization. Longer-term survival, including three-month mortality, could not be comprehensively assessed from the available records. Future prospective studies should incorporate standardized 30- and 90-day survival follow-up.

Finally, secondary and sensitivity analyses were exploratory without correction for multiple comparisons, several confidence intervals were wide, and the multivariable model was explanatory rather than a clinical prediction instrument and has not been externally validated.

In this Western Romanian cohort, PF positivity identified a distinct clinical, biochemical, and microbiological phenotype and was associated with greater unadjusted in-hospital morbidity and mortality. Its independent association with the composite outcome remained uncertain, whereas healthcare-associated or nosocomial acquisition was independently associated with adverse in-hospital outcomes and coincided with a greater burden of Gram-negative and multidrug-resistant organisms. Acquisition setting and local resistance ecology should inform empirical antimicrobial therapy, negative culture should not delay source control when pleural infection is otherwise established, and prospective multicenter studies using standardized sampling, molecular diagnostics, treatment pathways, temporal definitions, and harmonized component-level outcomes are required to validate these findings [ 2 , 18 ].

5. Conclusions A positive aerobic pleural culture identified a clinically distinct subgroup with more comorbidity, nosocomial acquisition, frank empyema, severe pleural biochemical abnormalities, and higher unadjusted in-hospital risk. Its adjusted association with the composite outcome remained uncertain and was sensitive to how temporal eligibility and outcome timing were handled. Healthcare-associated/nosocomial acquisition was independently associated with the composite and coincided with a greater burden of Gram-negative and multidrug-resistant organisms. These findings support systematic early pleural sampling, acquisition-specific empirical therapy, explicit component-level outcome reporting, and prospective multicenter validation using standardized laboratory and timing definitions.

BACKGROUND: Pleural infection requires early identification of individuals who are unlikely to respond to antibiotic therapy and may require drainage. Although several algorithms-Light's classification, the American College of Chest Physicians (ACCP) consensus statement, and the British Thoracic Society (BTS) 2003 and 2023 guidelines-are available, their predictive performance remains uncertain.

METHODS: This retrospective diagnostic accuracy study analyzed individuals with pleural infection treated at two municipal hospitals between 2017 and 2023. Missing data were handled using multiple imputation. The outcome, the need for drainage, was defined as chest tube insertion, video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery, repeated thoracentesis with intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy, open decortication, or death attributable to pleural infection. The predictive performance of the four algorithms was evaluated using sensitivity and specificity. RESULTS: Of the 215 individuals included, 57.7% experienced the outcome.

Sensitivity/specificity were 70.9/74.7% for Light's classification, 85.5/46.5% for ACCP statement, 53.1/85.9% for BTS 2003 guideline, and 68.1/70.4% for BTS 2023 guideline. Thus, ACCP statement showed the highest sensitivity but lowest specificity, whereas BTS 2003 demonstrated the opposite pattern. CONCLUSIONS: The choice of algorithms should depend on clinical context: ACCP statement may be preferred when minimizing missed cases is critical, whereas BTS 2003 guideline may be more appropriate for older adults or persons with frailty, where avoiding unnecessary invasive procedures is a priority. Timisoara, Romania. Background: Pleural infection remains associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and frequent treatment escalation. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated routinely available prognostic factors associated with adverse clinical outcomes in adults with pleural infection, including complicated parapneumonic effusion and pleural empyema. Methods: PubMed, Scopus,

Web of Science Core Collection, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to 6 July 2026. Studies evaluating routinely available clinical, biochemical, microbiological, pleural fluid, radiological, or composite prognostic factors were included. Methodological quality was assessed using the

Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Comparable data were synthesized using random-effects meta-analysis. Results: Thirty studies involving 8443 participants were included. The evaluated outcomes comprised treatment failure, short-term mortality, need for surgery, intensive care unit admission, recurrence, readmission, and length of hospital stay. Five studies (877 participants) contributed to the RAPID score meta-analysis. High-risk RAPID classification was associated with greater short-term mortality than combined low- and intermediate-risk classification (RR 4.52, 95% CI 2.71-7.55; primary OR

6.09, 95% CI 3.25-11.38; I2 = 0% for the OR analysis). In a limited meta-analysis of three studies (1239 participants), each 10-year increase in age was associated with higher odds of short-term mortality (OR 1.54, 95% CI

1.02-2.30; I2 = 30.4%); however, mortality was assessed in hospital in two studies and at 90 days in one study. Additional prognostic factors associated with adverse outcomes included comorbidity burden, renal dysfunction, hypoalbuminemia, serial C-reactive protein trajectories, bacteremia, pleural fluid biochemical markers, pleural thickening, loculation, and delayed or ineffective drainage, although heterogeneous reporting precluded further quantitative synthesis. Conclusions: The RAPID score is the most consistently supported routinely available predictor of short-term mortality in adults with pleural infection. Increasing age may also be prognostic, but its pooled estimate is based on only three studies with different mortality windows and should be interpreted cautiously. Future prospective multicenter studies using standardized outcome definitions are needed to validate additional prognostic markers and improve risk-guided clinical decision-making.

BACKGROUND: Although the RAPID score (renal, age, purulence, infection source, and dietary factors) is a validated predictor of mortality in pleural infection, the prognostic value of laboratory measurements obtained during early treatment remains uncertain. We evaluated whether day 3 laboratory markers, particularly blood urea nitrogen (BUN), were associated with failure to return to the pre-admission residence or care environment.

METHODS: This multicenter prospective observational study included 81 patients with pleural infection across 13 hospitals in Japan. Patients with complete baseline and day 3 data for BUN, C-reactive protein (CRP), albumin, and creatinine were included in the primary analysis. Multivariable Firth logistic regression models evaluated each day 3 laboratory marker after adjustment for its corresponding baseline value, age, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status. An exploratory sensitivity analysis excluded patients deemed unfit for surgery at baseline. The primary outcome was failure to return to the pre-admission residence or care environment at the end of the index hospitalization.

RESULTS: Among 81 patients, 25 (30.9%) did not return to their pre-admission residence or care environment. Day 3 BUN was not significantly associated with failure to return in the primary analysis [adjusted odds ratio (OR) per 5 mg/dL, 1.12; 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.91-1.47; P=0.30]. Day 3 CRP, albumin, and creatinine were also not significantly associated with the outcome. Older age was significantly associated with failure to return in all four models. In the exploratory sensitivity cohort of 70 patients, higher day 3 BUN was associated with failure to return (adjusted OR per 5 mg/dL, 1.60; 95% CI: 1.08-2.62; P=0.02).

CONCLUSIONS: Day 3 BUN and other routinely measured laboratory markers were not significantly associated with discharge disposition in the primary adjusted analysis. The association observed for day 3 BUN in the restricted sensitivity analysis should be considered hypothesis-generating and requires validation. © AME Publishing Company. BACKGROUND: Advances in the non-surgical management of pleural infection using intrapleural alteplase and DNase have reshaped treatment strategies. While twice-daily intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy (IPFT) is commonly used, evidence supporting once-daily regimens remains limited. We aimed to describe real-world outcomes associated with once- and twice-daily IPFT regimens and to compare their efficacy and safety, including outcomes among patients receiving modified alteplase doses.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study of patients diagnosed with pleural infection across three tertiary referral hospitals in Singapore. Clinical, radiological, and biochemical data were analysed. Logistic regression models were used to evaluate the association between dosing frequency, dose modification, and treatment outcomes.

RESULTS: A total of 266 patients were included. The mean age was 64 years, with a median Charlson Comorbidity Index of 3 and median RAPID (renal, age, purulence, infection source, dietary factors) score of 3. Twice-daily dosing was used in 238 patients (89.5%), while 28 patients (10.5%) received once-daily dosing. Alteplase dosing was 10 mg in 132 patients and modified (<10 mg) in 131 patients. Overall treatment success was 83.1%, with no significant difference between twice-daily and once-daily regimens (81.9% vs. 92.9%, P=0.19). On logistic regression analysis, dosing frequency was not significantly associated with treatment success or 30-day mortality. There were also no significant differences in treatment success or bleeding complications between modified and standard-dose alteplase regimens.

CONCLUSIONS: In this multicentre retrospective cohort, once-daily IPFT achieved clinical outcomes comparable to twice-daily regimens. Modified alteplase dosing (<10 mg) was similarly effective, and earlier initiation of therapy appeared to be associated with improved treatment success. Prospective studies are needed to define optimal dosing strategies, particularly in Asian populations where data remain limited. © AME Publishing Company. This retrospective study aimed to describe the clinical characteristics and outcomes associated with community-acquired pleural infection (CAPI) and hospital-acquired pleural infection (HAPI) in a large Chinese tertiary-care hospital in Beijing over 11 years. The study included 832 patients, of whom 84.9% had HAPI. The most common cause of CAPI was pneumonia and pleurisy, whereas the most common cause of HAPI was trauma or chest surgery.

The predisposing factors with statistically significant differences between HAPI and CAPI included the presence of an abdominal indwelling catheter (P = 0.012), thoracic cavity drainage (⩾ 10 days) (P = 0.003), and use of broad-spectrum antibiotics (P = 0.002). Staphylococcus epidermidis (24.76%) and Streptococcus species (27.00%) were the most common Gram-positive bacteria in HAPI and CAPI, respectively, whereas Acinetobacter baumannii (8.61%) and Escherichia coli (4.38%) were the most common Gram-negative pathogens in HAPI and CAPI, respectively. Virtually any Gram-positive bacteria were resistant to linezolid and vancomycin, except Enterococcus faecium displaying resistance to vancomycin (9.88%). The 30-day mortality after the onset of pleural infection was 13.1%.

Multivariable logistic regression analysis suggested that intensive care unit (ICU) admission, solid tumors, chronic renal failure, and a decreased serum albumin level were independent risk factors for pleural infection. No statistically significant difference in mortality was observed between patients with CAPI (11.9%) and those with HAPI (13.3%). Differences were noted in clinical characteristics between HAPI and CAPI. The findings might guide empirical treatments and help improve infection control strategies. © 2026. Higher Education Press. Intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy (IPFT), also known as intrapleural enzymatic therapy (IET), has been utilized for decades to treat pleural infections by expediting drainage in patients with pleural organization. The successful MIST2 trial demonstrated that IPFT improves pleural opacification, reduces hospital stays, and decreases short-term surgical referrals. Despite significant progress, gaps remain in identification of the optimal fibrinolytic agents, dosing, and safety improvements. IPFT is generally recommended for patients with loculation and failed pleural drainage, with a consensus panel advocating for combined tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) and DNase therapy. How each agent may affect the activity or function of the other in the combination remains unclear. While IPFT can reduce the need for surgical intervention, there are relatively few comparative clinical trials to guide initial therapy. Emerging low-dose IPFT treatment approaches may benefit patients who are poor surgical candidates. Personalized IPFT candidate approaches, such as the Fibrinolytic

Potential Assay (FPA), could refine dosing and improve outcomes. Additionally, biomarkers like pleural fluid PAI-1 and suPAR concentrations may predict clinical outcomes and guide treatment. New therapeutic agents, including PAI-1 inhibiting peptides and mesothelial profibrogenic targets, are under investigation to enhance IPFT efficacy. These advances hold promise for improving the management of pleural infections and other forms of pleural organization. © 2025. The Author(s). PURPOSE: Severe community-acquired pneumonia (sCAP) is associated with high morbidity and mortality, and whilst European and non-European guidelines are available for community-acquired pneumonia, there are no specific guidelines for sCAP. METHODS: The European Respiratory Society (ERS), European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM), European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious

Diseases (ESCMID), and Latin American Thoracic Association (ALAT) launched a task force to develop the first international guidelines for sCAP. The panel comprised a total of 18 European and four non-European experts, as well as two methodologists. Eight clinical questions for sCAP diagnosis and treatment were chosen to be addressed. Systematic literature searches were performed in several databases. Meta-analyses were performed for evidence synthesis, whenever possible. The quality of evidence was assessed with GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation). Evidence to Decision frameworks were used to decide on the direction and strength of recommendations.

RESULTS: Recommendations issued were related to diagnosis, antibiotics, organ support, biomarkers and co-adjuvant therapy. After considering the confidence in effect estimates, the importance of outcomes studied, desirable and undesirable consequences of treatment, cost, feasibility, acceptability of the intervention and implications to health equity, recommendations were made for or against specific treatment interventions.

CONCLUSIONS: In these international guidelines, ERS, ESICM, ESCMID, and ALAT provide evidence-based clinical practice recommendations for diagnosis, empirical treatment, and antibiotic therapy for sCAP, following the GRADE approach. Furthermore, current knowledge gaps have been highlighted and recommendations for future research have been made. © 2023. BACKGROUND: Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the leading bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) and a major source of morbidity and mortality in adults. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs) have substantially reduced invasive pneumococcal disease, but serotype replacement has led to shifts in pneumococcal CAP epidemiology. In addition, the identification of S. pneumoniae remains challenging. This study investigated pneumococcal serotype distribution, vaccine coverage, and the diagnostic yield of a serotype-specific urinary antigen detection assay (ssUAD) among adults with CAP in Switzerland between 2016 and 2021.

METHODS: Adult patients enrolled in the Swiss CAPNETZ cohort with available urine samples were analyzed using the Pfizer 24-serotype ssUAD assay. Results were compared with conventional diagnostic methods, including the pneumococcal urinary antigen test (pUAT) and cultures. Serotype distribution, vaccine coverage (PCV13, PCV15, PCV20 and PCV21), and temporal trends were assessed.

RESULTS: Among 234 CAP patients, S. pneumoniae was identified by conventional diagnostics (pUAT and cultures combined) in 37 (15.8%). The ssUAD was positive in 35 patients (15.0%). Among patients with available results from both conventional diagnostics and ssUAD (n = 161), the addition of ssUAD increased pneumococcal CAP detection from 18.6% to 29.2% (p = 0.036). Among ssUAD-positive patients, the most frequent serotypes detected by ssUAD were 3 (n = 12), 8 (n = 5), and 11A (n = 4). Based on ssUAD-derived serotype distribution, vaccine coverage was 54.3% for PCV13, 60.0% for PCV15, 91.4% for PCV20, and 85.7% for

PCV21. During 2020-2021, the proportion of serotypes not covered by PCV13 increased from 10/28 (35.7%) to 6/7 (85.7%) (p = 0.018). CONCLUSIONS: The addition of ssUAD improved S. pneumoniae detection beyond standard methods. Although based on a small number of cases, the shift toward non-PCV13 serotypes underscores the potential benefit of higher-valency vaccines such as PCV20 and PCV21 for adult pneumococcal disease prevention in Switzerland. © 2026. BACKGROUND: Influx of large numbers of neutrophils is characteristic of pleural infection; however, neutrophil behaviour is understudied. We designed an observational, multicohort study with the aims to discover and validate the association between neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), disease severity, 1-year survival and the extent of sonographic septations.

METHODS: We analysed five independent datasets across three countries. The PILOT cohort (UK, n=215) was used as a discovery cohort for the association of NETs with disease severity, with validation in four independent cohorts across three countries (UK, Greece and Italy, n=100). The PILOT cohort was further analysed to assess the association of NETs with 1-year survival and the development and extent of sonographic septations. A separate cohort (Oxford-Osler, UK, n=30) was used to assess the relationship between NETs and the need for intrapleural enzyme therapy as rescue treatment.

RESULTS: A 10-unit increase in NETs was associated with 13% higher odds of being in a higher RAPID score group (OR 1.13, 95% CI 1.02-1.27; p=0.02), and this association remained robust in the independent validation cohort (OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.11-1.40; p=0.0005). A 10-unit increase in NETs was also associated with a 15% higher risk of 1-year mortality (HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.01-1.32; p=0.04) independent of the RAPID score, and a 17% higher likelihood of sonographic septations (OR 1.17, 95% CI 1.01-1.37; p=0.04). Citrullinated fibrin was associated with septation severity (OR 1.10, 95% CI 1.04-1.16; p=0.00005).

CONCLUSIONS: Pleural fluid NETs are a biomarker of disease severity and 1-year mortality, in pleural infection. Future studies are required to assess the combination of NET-targeting strategies in combination with existing treatments. Copyright ©The authors 2026.
